# dtcloud_vm (Resource)

Manages a virtual machine.

This resource builds the machine, renames it, resizes it, changes its power state and destroys it.
Interfaces and volumes added after boot belong to `dtcloud_vm_network_interface` and
`dtcloud_vm_volume_attachment`.

## Example Usage

```terraform
resource "dtcloud_vm" "web" {
  name      = "web-01"
  flavor_id = data.dtcloud_flavors.small.flavors[0].id
  state     = "running"

  key_name  = dtcloud_ssh_key.deploy.name
  user_data = base64encode(file("${path.module}/cloud-init.yaml"))

  # Interfaces declared here are created with the machine and live and die with
  # it. Add one afterwards with dtcloud_vm_network_interface instead.
  network {
    uuid            = dtcloud_network.app.id
    security_groups = [dtcloud_security_group.web.id]

    fixed_ip {
      ip_version = 4
    }
  }

  # The boot disk is boot_index 0.
  block_device {
    boot_index            = 0
    volume_size           = 40
    source_type           = "image"
    device_type           = "disk"
    destination_type      = "volume"
    uuid                  = var.image_id
    volume_type           = "standard"
    delete_on_termination = true
  }
}
```

~> **At least one of `key_name`, `user_data` or `script` is required.** They are the only ways
credentials or a provisioning payload reach the guest. `user_data` and `script` cannot both be set:
the platform builds cloud-init from `script` only when `user_data` is absent, so the plan refuses
the combination instead of silently dropping the script.

-> On a Linux image, set `username`, `hostname` and `disable_root` in `script`. They are optional
only because Windows template images ignore them, and the apply warns when a Linux `script` leaves
any of them out.

-> Leave `fixed_ip` out for the usual case: the provider asks for one address and the platform
allocates it. The addresses actually assigned are reported back into the `network` blocks.

## Schema

### Required

- `flavor_id` (String) ID of the flavor (sizing). Changing this resizes the instance in place. Unless enable_hot_plug is true the platform requires the instance to be stopped first, so the provider stops it, resizes and returns it to the configured power state — a plan that does this is the one where `status` also shows as (known after apply).
- `name` (String) Name of the virtual machine. Can be changed in place.

### Optional

- `block_device` (Block List) Block devices to attach at boot. The boot disk is the entry with boot_index 0. At least one is required. Changing this forces a new resource to be created. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--block_device))
- `enable_hot_plug` (Boolean) Allow live vCPU/memory resize on the instance. With this on, changing flavor_id does not power-cycle the instance. Can be toggled after creation.
- `graceful_shutdown` (Boolean) When stopping, ask the guest to shut down (softStop) instead of cutting power (hardStop).
- `is_gpu_image` (Boolean) Set when booting a GPU image. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `key_name` (String) Name of an existing SSH key to inject, e.g. a dtcloud_ssh_key resource's name. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `network` (Block List) Network interfaces to attach at boot. At least one is required. Changing this forces a new resource to be created. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--network))
- `script` (Block List, Max: 1) Initial credentials applied to the guest at first boot. On a Linux image, set username, hostname and disable_root as well — they are optional only because Windows template images ignore them. Changing this forces a new resource to be created. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--script))
- `state` (String) Desired power state: running, stopped or shelved. Shelving releases compute resources while keeping the VM and its disks.
- `timeouts` (Block, Optional) (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--timeouts))
- `user_data` (String) Cloud-init user data. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.

### Read-Only

- `created_at` (String) When the VM was created, in RFC 3339 format.
- `flavor_name` (String) Human-readable name of the VM's flavor.
- `id` (String) The ID of this resource.
- `image` (String) Name of the image the VM was built from.
- `image_os_type` (String) OS family of the image, e.g. linux or windows.
- `last_modified` (String) When the VM was last modified, in RFC 3339 format.
- `metadata` (Map of String) Metadata the platform attaches to the instance, e.g. ha_enabled.
- `network_interface` (List of Object) Network interfaces currently attached to the VM. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--network_interface))
- `primary_ip` (String) Convenience shortcut: the primary IP of the first public interface, falling back to the first interface with an address.
- `ram` (String) Memory as reported by the API, e.g. "512 MB".
- `ssh_key` (String) Name of the SSH key injected into the VM.
- `status` (String) Current power/provisioning state, e.g. ACTIVE, SHUTOFF, ERROR.
- `task_state` (String) In-flight OpenStack task, empty when the VM is settled.
- `vcpus` (Number) Number of virtual CPUs.
- `volume` (List of Object) Volumes currently attached to the VM, including the boot disk. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--volume))

<a id="nestedblock--block_device"></a>
### Nested Schema for `block_device`

Required:

- `boot_index` (Number) Boot order. The boot disk is 0. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `delete_on_termination` (Boolean) Whether the device is deleted with the VM. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `destination_type` (String) One of: volume, local. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `device_type` (String) One of: cdrom, disk. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `source_type` (String) Where the device comes from. One of: blank, image, volume, backup. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `volume_size` (Number) Size in GB (1-8192). Can be increased in place; decreasing is not supported.
- `volume_type` (String) Storage policy / volume type the disk is created on. Can be changed in place.

Optional:

- `uuid` (String) ID of the source image, volume or backup. Omitted for blank devices. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.


<a id="nestedblock--network"></a>
### Nested Schema for `network`

Required:

- `uuid` (String) ID of the network to attach to. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.

Optional:

- `fixed_ip` (Block List) Fixed IPs on this interface. Omit to have one address allocated. Can be changed in place. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--network--fixed_ip))
- `port_security_enabled` (Boolean) Whether port security (and therefore security groups) applies to this interface. Defaults to the network's own setting. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `security_groups` (List of String) Security group IDs bound to this interface. Can be changed in place. Defaults to the project's default group.

<a id="nestedblock--network--fixed_ip"></a>
### Nested Schema for `network.fixed_ip`

Optional:

- `ip_address` (String) Specific address to request. Allocated by the platform when omitted, and reported back here either way.
- `ip_version` (Number) IP version, 4 or 6. Advisory on write — the platform allocates from the attached network; pin ip_address to choose an address. Reported back from the assigned address.



<a id="nestedblock--script"></a>
### Nested Schema for `script`

Required:

- `os` (String) Guest OS family. One of: linux, windows. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `password` (String, Sensitive) Initial password for the guest account. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.

Optional:

- `disable_root` (Boolean) Disable direct root login. Required in practice on Linux images; ignored by Windows template images. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `hostname` (String) Hostname to set inside the guest. Required in practice on Linux images; ignored by Windows template images. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.
- `username` (String) Account to create. Required in practice on Linux images; ignored by Windows template images. Changing this forces a new resource to be created.

## Behaviour worth knowing

* **What changes in place.** `name`, `flavor_id`, `state`, `enable_hot_plug`, and inside the blocks
  `network.security_groups`, `network.fixed_ip`, `block_device.volume_size` (increase only) and
  `block_device.volume_type`. Adding or removing a whole `network` or `block_device` block,
  `network.uuid`, `network.port_security_enabled`, the other `block_device` fields and the boot-time
  arguments `key_name`, `user_data`, `script` and `is_gpu_image` build a new machine.
* **Resizing.** With `enable_hot_plug = true` the flavor changes while the machine keeps running.
  Without it the platform refuses to resize a running instance, so the provider stops it, resizes it
  and returns it to the configured `state`. In a plan, the resize that power-cycles the machine is the
  one where `status` also shows as known after apply, and the apply warns that the machine was
  restarted.
* **Growing a disk does not grow the filesystem.** After `volume_size` increases, extend the partition
  and the filesystem inside the guest (`growpart` and `resize2fs`, or your filesystem's equivalent);
  the apply warns about it. `volume_size` cannot be decreased.
* **The guest does not see a changed `fixed_ip` at once.** The address moves on the port, but the
  operating system keeps the old one until its DHCP lease renews, and for good if the interface is
  configured statically. Renew the lease or reboot; the apply warns about it.
* **`port_security_enabled` has no default.** Left unset it is not sent, and the network decides. It
  cannot be `false` while `security_groups` is set on the same block.
* **Extra disks are matched by size and storage policy.** Beyond the boot disk the platform reports no
  order, so a `block_device` change is refused when two attached volumes look the same. Manage such
  disks with `dtcloud_vm_volume_attachment`.
* **What drift Terraform can see.** `name`, `flavor_id`, `state`, `key_name`, `enable_hot_plug`, the
  `network` blocks and the size, storage policy and delete-on-termination setting of each
  `block_device` are read back. `user_data`, `script` and `is_gpu_image` are not reported by any
  endpoint, so a change made to them outside Terraform stays invisible.
* **`network_interface` and `volume` are a snapshot** from the last refresh. Interfaces and volumes
  attached by other resources in the same apply appear after the next refresh.
* **One resource is one machine.** The API can create several machines in one call; this resource
  does not expose that. Use Terraform's `count` or `for_each`.

`state` is the power state Terraform keeps the machine in; a machine always boots running first.

| From | To | What the provider does |
|------|----|------------------------|
| `running` | `stopped` | `softStop`, or `hardStop` when `graceful_shutdown = false` |
| `stopped` | `running` | `start` |
| any | `shelved` | `shelve`, which releases the compute resources and keeps the machine and its disks |
| `shelved` | `running` | `unshelve` |
| `shelved` | `stopped` | `unshelve`, then stop |

## Timeouts

`create` defaults to 20 minutes, `update` to 10 minutes and `delete` to 15 minutes. Creating waits
for the machine to reach `ACTIVE`, and a resize stops and restarts it, so an update can take several
minutes. Override them with a `timeouts` block:

```terraform
resource "dtcloud_vm" "web" {
  # ...

  timeouts {
    create = "30m"
  }
}
```

## Import

```shell
# user_data, script and is_gpu_image are not reported by any endpoint: read the
# import notes before the first apply.
terraform import dtcloud_vm.web 4c9a1f37-8d25-4e60-b13f-6a7c2e5b9d88
```

Read back on import: `name`, `flavor_id`, `state`, `key_name`, `enable_hot_plug`, every interface as
a `network` block, and the boot disk as a `block_device` block. The boot disk's `source_type`,
`device_type` and `destination_type` are inferred, because the platform does not report them. Not
read back: `user_data`, `script`, `is_gpu_image`, `graceful_shutdown`, and disks attached after boot.

`user_data`, `script` and `is_gpu_image` force a new machine, so if the configuration sets them the
first plan after an import proposes a rebuild. Ignore them to keep the imported machine:

```terraform
resource "dtcloud_vm" "web" {
  # ...

  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [user_data, script, is_gpu_image]
  }
}
```

!> **Import a machine before attaching extra interfaces to it.** An import has no blocks to match
against, so every interface the machine has becomes a `network` block. If some of them belong to
`dtcloud_vm_network_interface` resources, the configuration declares fewer blocks than were
imported, and the first plan proposes to replace the machine.
